steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The cognitive approach focuses on internal mental processes: perception, memory, thinking, problem-solving, attention, and language. It treats the mind like a computer: input (sensory information) -> processing (thinking) -> output (behaviour).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Schemas: mental frameworks that organise knowledge and expectations. They help us process information quickly but can lead to biases and errors. Schemas develop through experience and affect how we interpret new information (e.g. Bartlett's 'War of the Ghosts' study showed participants distorted a story to fit their cultural schemas).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Cognitive biases: systematic errors in thinking that affect decisions and judgements. Confirmation bias: seeking information that confirms existing beliefs. Anchoring: relying too heavily on the first piece of information. Hindsight bias: 'I knew it all along' after an event. These biases are studied in forensic psychology and economics.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The cognitive approach and mental health: Beck's negative triad (negative views of self, world, future) maintains depression. Ellis's ABC model: Activating event -> Beliefs -> Consequences. Irrational beliefs cause emotional problems. CBT directly applies cognitive principles to treat mental health conditions.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Describe the key assumptions of the cognitive approach and explain how schemas influence behaviour. | Evaluate the cognitive approach, comparing it with the biological approach. | Explain how cognitive biases affect decision-making, giving examples.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Cognitive approach: mind = INFORMATION PROCESSOR. Input -> Processing -> Output. Schemas = mental frameworks. They HELP (quick processing) but can DISTORT (bias, stereotyping). Cognitive strengths = scientific + CBT. Limitations = machine reductionism + ignores biology + based on inference.
